\chapter{Naming the Land --- Village, Hill, Valley, Lake, Mountain}
\label{ch:la-tierra}
\hlchaptermodality{292}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the village, a hill, a valley, a lake and a mountain in Spanish, and say where I am from.}

Complete ES-C292-montana: name all five features of a landscape and place a village among them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el pueblo]{el pueblo — the place and the people, one word}

\label{lesson:ES-C292-pueblo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: where does \emph{bosque} come from? (Germanic, not Latin.) And what was \emph{ramus}? (A branch.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — what a small one is mostly made of.
  \item el vecino — who lives in it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PUE-blo}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ue} is one slide, and the \emph{b} between vowels is the soft one. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pueblo} — \textquotedblleft{}the village,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the people.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{populus} meant the people, the citizen body. Spanish kept that sense and added the other one, so \emph{el pueblo} is both the settlement and everybody in it, and Spanish does not usually feel the need to say which.

\emph{Populus} is generous in English. Something \textbf{popular} belongs to the people. A \textbf{population} is the whole of them counted. Anything \textbf{public} is theirs rather than private — \emph{publicus} is \emph{populus} worn down. And \textbf{people} itself came through French from the same Latin, so the English and the Spanish word are the same word, three roads apart.

Watch the \emph{ue}. Latin's short \emph{o} in \emph{populus} broke into \emph{ue} in Spanish, the same way the short \emph{e} broke into \emph{ie} in \emph{cielo}. Once you can hear those two breaks, a very large number of Spanish words stop being surprises.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One word doing two jobs, which is a bargain.

You can now name where somebody is from, and the answer is also a claim about who they are. That is a genuinely useful thing to be able to say when you are meeting people, and it costs one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pueblo}
  \item \emph{mi pueblo}
  \item \emph{pueblo}, \emph{popular}, \emph{público} — the same Latin three times
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{populus} mean? (The people.) What two things does \emph{pueblo} name? (The village and the people in it.) And what did Latin's short \emph{o} become? (\emph{Ue}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la colina]{la colina — the same rising that is in excel}

\label{lesson:ES-C292-colina}



\begin{quote}
Two back: which of the tree words was Germanic? (\emph{El bosque}.) And what does \emph{pueblo} name besides the village? (The people.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pueblo — often sitting on one of these.
  \item el bosque — what is often growing on it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-LI-na}, stress in the middle. Both \emph{l} sounds are bright and forward. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la colina} — \textquotedblleft{}the hill.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{collis}, a hill, and behind it an old root that simply meant to rise or to stand up. That root went everywhere.

To \textbf{excel} is \emph{ex-} plus \emph{cellere}, to rise out above the rest. To \textbf{culminate} is to reach the \textbf{culmen}, the summit. And the plain English \textbf{hill} is a cousin too, arriving through Germanic rather than Latin — the same ancient rising, split between the two halves of your vocabulary.

The \emph{-ina} on the end is a softening, the same shape as in \emph{cocina}. Spanish tends to take a blunt Latin word and hand it a warmer ending, and \emph{collis} to \emph{colina} is that habit in one step.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and between them you can place a settlement in a landscape.

\emph{El pueblo} and \emph{la colina} are the beginning of being able to answer \textquotedblleft{}where are you from?\textquotedblright{} with something more than a name — which is exactly what you do when you meet somebody and the name alone is not enough.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la colina}
  \item \emph{el pueblo en la colina}
  \item \emph{colina}, then \emph{excel} — both of them rising
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{collis}? (A hill.) What does the old root behind it mean? (To rise.) And which two English words still rise? (\emph{Excel}, \emph{culminate}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el valle]{el valle — the low half of the pair}

\label{lesson:ES-C292-valle}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what was \emph{collis}? (A hill.) And what two things does \emph{el pueblo} name? (The village and its people.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la colina — the opposite shape.
  \item la nieve — what comes down into one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VA-lle}, stress on the first part. The \emph{v} is said with both lips, close to a soft \emph{b}, and the \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} sound. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el valle} — \textquotedblleft{}the valley.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vallis}, and English has it twice over. \textbf{Valley} came through French, carrying the extra syllable. \textbf{Vale} is the same word arriving earlier and shorter, which is why it survives mostly in place names and poetry.

\textbf{Avalanche} belongs here too, though it took a detour: it is from a dialect of the Alps, built on the idea of descending — \emph{a val}, to the valley. What an avalanche is named for is not the snow, but where the snow ends up.

The \emph{v} is worth a moment. In Spanish it is not the English \emph{v} made with teeth and lip; it is made with both lips, and in most positions it is barely distinguishable from \emph{b}. Spanish speakers who have not been taught spelling mix the two up in writing for exactly that reason.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and they are starting to describe a place rather than list things.

\emph{El pueblo}, \emph{la colina}, \emph{el valle}. High ground, low ground, and somewhere for people to live between them. That is a landscape, and you can now put a name to one when somebody asks where you grew up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el valle}
  \item \emph{la colina}, then \emph{el valle} — up, then down
  \item \emph{el pueblo del valle}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{vallis}? (A valley.) Which two English words are both from it? (\emph{Valley} and \emph{vale}.) And how is the Spanish \emph{v} made? (With both lips, near a soft \emph{b}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el lago]{el lago — and the gap it leaves in a page}

\label{lesson:ES-C292-lago}



\begin{quote}
Quick pass: what was \emph{vallis}? (A valley.) What was \emph{collis}? (A hill.) And what was \emph{populus}? (The people.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what one is made of.
  \item el valle — where one usually sits.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{LA-go}, stress on the first part. The \emph{g} before \emph{o} is hard, and softens a little between vowels. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el lago} — \textquotedblleft{}the lake.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{lacus}, standing water. English \textbf{lake} is the same word through French, and \textbf{lagoon} arrived later through Italian \emph{laguna}, which is \emph{lacuna} worn smooth.

That last one is the interesting turn. A \textbf{lacuna} in Latin is a pool or a pit, and scholars borrowed it for a hole in a manuscript — a place where the text has gone missing. So the word for a small lake became the word for a gap in a page, because both are an absence with an edge round it.

\emph{Lacus} also went north on its own and turned up in English as \textbf{loch} and \textbf{lough} through the Celtic languages, which is why the map of Scotland and Ireland is covered in a Spanish word nobody there would recognise as one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the landscape now has water in it.

\emph{El pueblo}, \emph{la colina}, \emph{el valle}, \emph{el lago}. You could describe most of the places people are actually from with these four and nothing else, which is not bad for four words that each came with an English relative attached.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el lago}
  \item \emph{el lago del valle}
  \item \emph{el pueblo}, \emph{la colina}, \emph{el valle}, \emph{el lago}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{lacus}? (Standing water.) What is a \emph{lacuna} in a text? (A gap where something is missing.) And why is it called that? (It was a pool first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la montaña]{la montaña — the hill inside amount}

\label{lesson:ES-C292-montana}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{lacus}? (Standing water.) What was \emph{vallis}? (A valley.) And what was \emph{collis}? (A hill.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la colina — the smaller version.
  \item la nieve — what is on top of one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mon-TA-ña}, stress in the middle. The \emph{ñ} is one sound, not two: the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la montaña} — \textquotedblleft{}the mountain.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mons}, and in its other forms \textbf{montem}, a hill. Spanish built \emph{montaña} on it; English took \textbf{mountain} through French from the same place.

Then \emph{mons} went quietly into a set of English words that have stopped looking like hills at all. Something \textbf{paramount} is \emph{par a mont}, up above. To \textbf{surmount} is to get over the top. To \textbf{amount} to something is to climb to it — which is why a bill amounts to a figure, as though the total were a summit. A \textbf{montage} is things mounted, stacked up.

The \emph{ñ} is the one letter here that Latin did not have. It began as a scribe's shortcut for a doubled \emph{n}: rather than write the second one in full, they set a tiny \emph{n} over the first to save space, and that tiny mark hardened into the tilde. \emph{Montanea} to \emph{montaña} is that shortcut, frozen.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el pueblo}, \emph{la colina}, \emph{el valle}, \emph{el lago}, \emph{la montaña}.

Together they are a place, and a place is what most people mean when they tell you where they are from. You started this run able to give a name; you can now give a landscape as well, which is the difference between an introduction and a conversation.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la montaña}
  \item \emph{la colina}, then \emph{la montaña} — small, then large
  \item all five — \emph{el pueblo}, \emph{la colina}, \emph{el valle}, \emph{el lago}, \emph{la montaña}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{mons}? (A hill.) What does \emph{paramount} say, taken apart? (Up above.) And where did the \emph{ñ} come from? (A scribe's tiny second \emph{n}, set over the first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
